newsitem.title: USA: Poll gives poor marks to Ill. Sen. Moseley-Braun.
newsitem.headline: Poll gives poor marks to Ill. Sen. Moseley-Braun.

text.p: Sen. Carol Moseley-Braun, an Illinois Democrat who was the first black woman ever elected to the Senate, fared poorly against potential Republican opponents in a Chicago Tribune poll published Sunday.

Of the 711 Illinois voters surveyed, 49 percent said they would like to see someone new elected to Moseley-Braun's senate seat when her initial term is up in 1998, while 33 percent wanted her re-elected. Another 18 percent were not sure.

The poll commissioned by the Tribune showed Moseley-Braun's favourable rating climbed to 37 percent from 32 percent nine months ago, but still lagged far behind potential Republican opponents. Overall, 40 percent had an unfavourable view of her, 18 percent had no opinion and 5 percent had never heard of her. The loss of support for Moseley-Braun was particularly pronounced among white suburban women who were a key constituency in her upset victory in 1992.

Popular Illinois Gov. Jim Edgar, who has not decided on whether to seek re-election or vie for Moseley-Braun's senate seat, was seen by the Tribune as a potentially easy winner against her with a favourable rating of 64 percent. Two other state Republican office-holders also bettered her in the poll.

Moseley-Braun, who had held low-level posts in state and county government prior to winning the senate seat, has been dogged by various controversies, including a visit with Nigerian dictator Gen. Sani Abacha shortly after her election that drew a rebuke from the State Department. She also has faced lawsuits alleging various misuses of campaign funds, and admitted to improperly billing Medicare to house her mother in a nursing home.

President Clinton was due to appear at a fund-raiser this week on behalf of Moseley-Braun, who has nearly wiped out a large campaign debt left over from 1992 and is seeking funds to run for re-election. Chicago Mayor Richard Daley has also come out in support for her.
The poll commissioned by the newspaper had an error margin of plus or minus 4 percent.
